item.description: Exhibit will be open between Tuesday, November 3, 2026 to Thursday, December 24, 2026.Open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from 1:00 p.m. - 4 p.m.No appointment needed.Located in the Beckman Room, first floor of Beckman Institute.On Wednesday, November 4, the exhibition will be open during the preshow for Professor Katie Bouman's Watson Lecture (6–7 p.m.).Celebrate 90 years of discovery, innovation, and exploration.Join us in celebrating 90 years since Caltech founded the Jet Propulsion Laboratory with a visit to Dare Mighty Things: From Rocketry to Space Exploration at Caltech JPL, a new exhibition presented by the Caltech and JPL Archives in the Beckman Room at Beckman Institute.Explore nine decades of scientific ambition and technological innovation through historic documents, spacecraft models, and concept paintings drawn from the Caltech and JPL Archives. From JPL's early roots in rocketry to its pioneering work in planetary science, Earth sciences, and astronomy, the exhibition traces the ideas, discoveries, and engineering achievements that have helped expand our understanding of the universe. Discover the history behind the exploration—and the vision that continues to propel it forward.

item.title: Watson Lecture - Katie Bouman: Illuminating the Hidden Universe with Physics and AI
item.description: Katie Bouman, associate professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator Advance registration for this event has closed. Guests who have not pre-registered are invited to join our standby line. We recommend you arrive no later than 6:50 p.m. for standby. If you registered, please bring your ticket (paper or electronic).A recording of the event will be made available on our YouTube channel. Join our mailing list to receive the latest on public events at Caltech. Thank you for your interest!About the TalkSome of the most iconic images in modern science were never captured by a camera in the traditional sense. Instead, they were inferred from indirect and incomplete measurements, using a careful combination of physics, prior knowledge, and computation. In this talk, Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; and Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator; will explore how physics and artificial intelligence (AI) are working together to illuminate parts of the universe that are difficult—or even fundamentally impossible—to observe directly. It begins with the story of black hole imaging, where theory long predicted what we should see, and where confidence came not from a single image, but from the consistency of features across many reconstructions of the same data. This kind of inference is not unique to extreme astrophysics, but it also underlies how researchers form images in familiar technologies they rely on every day. In this talk, Bouman will demonstrate how simple assumptions can take us far, but she will also explain where these assumptions begin to limit what we can learn, and how modern AI methods provide new ways to explore richer possibilities while still respecting physical laws. More broadly, this talk explores a shift in scientific imaging: As we push the boundaries of observation, images are increasingly constructed rather than simply captured, and understanding how they are made is essential to interpreting what they show.Visit Katie Bouman's Watson Lecture page for more information.Evening Schedule6 p.m. — Activities and music. Food, drinks, and books available for purchase.7 p.m. — Doors open.7:30 p.m. — Talk and Q&A.8:30 p.m. — Post-talk concessions and conversation.The live event is in-person and a recording will be made available on our Youtube channel.About the SeriesFor more than 100 years, the Watson Lectures have brought the wonder of Caltech research and discovery to the public.Free and open to the public, the Watson Lecture Series offers a unique and accessible opportunity to learn more about cutting-edge science directly from Caltech's premier researchers. Then head inside to hear a stimulating talk and stay to ask your burning questions.Many past Watson Lectures are available on Caltech's YouTube channel.

item.title: Leviathan Unchained: Rethinking the Framers on Executive Power
item.description: John Ferejohn, (HSS Faculty 1972–1983) Samuel Tilden Professor of Law, Emeritus, NYU School of Law Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, Rea A. and Lela G. Axline Professor of Business Economics and Director of the Ronald and Maxine Linde Institute of Economic and Management Sciences, Caltech The framers of the Constitution wanted a limited and small government. In conversation with Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, John Ferejohn will consider three questions: Was the framers' focus on controlling the legislature, rather than the executive, a fundamental flaw? Why has the growth of the executive branch's power accelerated over the last three decades? And how much of this constitutional dynamic results from domestic forces (like race or income inequality) versus international imperatives (such as war or industrial politics)? There will be time for questions from the audience at the end of the session.The HSS 60th Anniversary Celebration will continue on Saturday, November 7, with a full day of presentations by HSS alumni followed by conversations with current HSS faculty, organized around four themes showcasing the reach and relevance of our expertise. Topics will include everything from AI and democracy to space sustainability, data, and the future of higher education. To view the compete program and register for activities, please visit hss.caltech.edu/hss60.This event is free and open to the public.REGISTRATION IS REQUIRED

item.title: Movies That Matter: LIGO Documentary "Cosmic Coda"
item.description: Click here to register and view the trailer.Caltech proudly presents Cosmic Coda (Astrophysics for Dairy Cows), a film by MJ Doherty about the teamwork required to develop LIGO over 40 years (minus a 30-year hole in the middle). This monumental NSF-funded project was developed on both the Caltech and MIT campuses.The film, featuring a haunting score by Room Full of Teeth, will be screened for free in Beckman Auditorium on Monday, November 9, 2026, at 7:30 PM with a panel and Q & A following featuring Caltech professors Kip Thorne and Rana Adhikari and the film's director.Though Thorne, whose work on LIGO dates to 1968, is not in the film, he was the theorist for the project; an equal partner in the conceptualization and design of LIGO.Thorne will convey a contextualized understanding of the processes that led to he and his two colleagues receiving their Nobel Prizes.Reservations are highly recommendedPlease note: Reservations are good until 15 minutes before the event starts, at which time people in the standby line will be allowed to take unclaimed seats.Click here to register and view the trailer.Presented by Caltech's Division of Physics, Mathematics, and Astronomy and Movies That Matter.

item.title: A Conversation with Author Jeff VanderMeer
item.description: Jeff VanderMeer Called "the weird Thoreau" by The New Yorker, Jeff VanderMeer has reshaped contemporary environmental fiction with the strange ecologies and uncanny terrain of his Southern Reach series and Borne novels. His latest work, Absolution (part four of the Southern Reach series), is a New York Times bestseller and a finalist for the Los Angeles Times Book Prize. VanderMeer has also written environmental nonfiction for Time, The Nation, the Los Angeles Times, Esquire, and other publications. Join us for an evening in which he will discuss his fiction, his environmental activism, and how powerful storytelling can challenge the way we think about wilderness, biotechnology, and the world beyond the human.This event is supported by a gift from the late Caltech trustee James F. Rothenberg to support seminars in honor of his wife, Anne Rothenberg.

item.title: Campus History & Architectural Tour
item.description: This Event is Full. To register for future tours, please RSVP here.Join a tour led by volunteer docents from CHATS (Campus History & Architectural Tour Service). Discover how the original academic buildings and high-tech laboratories of Caltech, one of the world's foremost institutions of science and engineering, created an architectural footprint that relates to the surrounding community. After a brief visit to the Athenaeum, Gordon Kaufmann's Mediterranean eclectic faculty club completed in 1930, the historic tour will explore Caltech's original campus. Participants will see how Bertram Goodhue & Goodhue Associates using shaded portals, stucco walls, Roman arches and water features to set the tone for a campus of great beauty so that scientists and engineers would become more aware of the aesthetic values of life.NOTE: This is a strenuous walk and is not suitable for people with strollers, walkers or children. The total distance is approximately 1⅓ miles and includes flights of steps. Tours last from 1½ to 2 hours. Low-heeled shoes are advised.The Athenaeum parking lot is reserved for members and guests of members only. Visitors have two hours of free parking on Hill Avenue and California Boulevard.

item.title: Watson Lecture - Sarkis Mazmanian: Trust Your Gut: Microbiome Influences on Brain Health and Disease
item.description: Sarkis Mazmanian, Luis B. and Nelly Soux professor of microbiology; Merkin Institute Professor Advance registration for Mazmanian's talk is full. Guests who have not registered are still welcome to attend the preshow, which does not require registration, beginning at 6 p.m., featuring food, music, and interactive displays.After the preshow, non-ticketed guests interested in attending the talk may join our standby line by 6:50 p.m.About the TalkTrust Your Gut: Microbiome Influences on Brain Health and DiseaseWhile the brain receives visual, auditory, olfactory, and other sensory information, the majority of molecular input to the brain comes through our gastrointestinal tract. Rather than being isolated, the brain is in constant communication with the gut via neuronal connections, the immune system, or intestinal hormones. Remarkably, many molecules produced by gut bacteria of the human microbiome can be found in the brain.In this talk, Sarkis Mazmanian, the Luis B. & Nelly Soux Professor of Microbiology and a Merkin Institute Professor, will share his laboratory's work on the fascinating and enigmatic gut–brain connection and its impacts on behavior and brain function. Harnessing the link between gut bacteria to the brain may uncover causes for disorders such as Parkinson's disease, and it may also enable therapies based on entirely novel biological principles.Evening Schedule6 p.m. — Activities and music. item.title: Terra String Quartet
item.description: "This young quartet displayed great musicality and superb ensemble playing throughout the performance…" - Hyde Park HeraldThe Terra String Quartet has performed at numerous festivals and venues across the world, and is deeply invested in education and community work. In addition to winning the Naumburg Chamber Music Competition in 2025, the quartet also won top prizes at Bordeaux and Wigmore Hall; in 2023 at Melbourne and Osaka; in 2022 the Fischoff, and also the Anderson Career Development Prize at Banff.The quartet is composed of graduates of The Juilliard School, The New England Conservatory, Harvard University, and The Curtis Institute of Music, four musicians known for their sincere storytelling, commitment to artistic excellence, and versatile approach to repertoire, and they strive to foster conversation and genuine human connection through their performances and pedagogy. Their name is a nod to their multicultural origins — together, this foursome represents four continents and speaks six languages.PROGRAM:Haydn – Quartet in C Major, Op. 54, No. 2, Hob.
